steps.explanationAfterStep: A cheletropic reaction: the two σ bonds that break both end on one atom, sulfur. Six electrons move round the five-membered ring (two σ pairs and one π pair). The loss of a stable gas, SO₂, makes it downhill on heating. With the diene's four electrons and the sulfur's pair taking part suprafacially, the ring opens disrotatory: cis-2,5-dimethylsulfolene gives only (E,E)-hexa-2,4-diene. The app does not check stereochemistry yet, so the drawings carry no wedges.

title: Cheletropic extrusion of SO₂
subtitle: 3-Sulfolene loses sulfur dioxide to give buta-1,3-diene
references: Clayden, Greeves and Warren, Organic Chemistry, 2nd edition (Oxford University Press), chapter 34
Fleming, Pericyclic Reactions, 2nd edition (Oxford Chemistry Primers, Oxford University Press)

sulfolene.caption: 3-sulfolene (2,5-dihydrothiophene 1,1-dioxide)
hintTiers: Both bonds that break go to the same atom, sulfur: a cheletropic reaction. What does the sulfur keep, and where do the electrons of the other C–S bond go?
One C–S pair stays with sulfur as a lone pair (SO₂ has one); the other C–S pair becomes a new C=C, and the ring C=C moves across to the other end. Three arrows.

Arrow 1: from one C–S bond to a lone pair on sulfur. Arrow 2: from the ring C=C π bond to the bond between the CH₂ that just lost sulfur and its neighbour. Arrow 3: from the other C–S bond to the bond between its CH₂ and its neighbour.
sulfolene.learnerPrompt: On heating, both C–S bonds break at once and sulfur dioxide leaves. Draw the single step.

misconceptions.arrowPattern: σ C1-S5 -> lp S5; σ C4-S5 -> lp S5
misconceptions.feedbackMessage: Both C–S pairs going to sulfur would leave the four carbons with two electrons too few. SO₂ keeps one lone pair on sulfur; the other C–S pair stays on the carbons as a new π bond.
The S=O bonds stay: SO₂ leaves with both oxygens. Only the two C–S bonds break.

partialProgressMessages.feedbackMessage: Right: one C–S pair stays on sulfur. In the same step the other C–S bond breaks too, its pair making a C=C, and the ring C=C shifts across. Two more arrows.

mechanismSummary: In a cheletropic reaction two σ bonds to one atom form or break together. 3-Sulfolene, a stable crystalline solid, loses SO₂ on heating to give buta-1,3-diene; the reverse, butadiene + SO₂ at room temperature, is how sulfolene is made. So sulfolene is a safe, weighable source of gaseous butadiene: heated with maleic anhydride in xylene, it releases the diene slowly and the Diels–Alder adduct forms in the same flask. The ring opening is disrotatory (6 electrons, thermal, linear cheletropic), explained, not drawn. The app does not check stereochemistry yet, so the drawings carry no wedges.
